title: Who is a true sati
hook: not those who burn on the husband's pyre, but those who live in faithfulness (Suhi Var M3, ang 787)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the burning world, and a prayer for it to be saved by whatever door it can be saved. Your line was by any door. Which small door did you walk through? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-five.

Some words carry a compliment and a wound at the same time. Sati is one. Around Guru Amar Das, it could name a faithful, virtuous woman. It could also name a widow who burned on her husband's funeral pyre, a practice found in parts of the society he lived in. A grieving woman could be pushed toward the fire by the very word that honored her. In the Var of Raga Suhi, Guru Amar Das takes that word and changes who it belongs to.
screen: `A COMPLIMENT AND A WOUND.` → `THE FUNERAL PYRE.` → `THE GURU TAKES THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here are his saloks, paraphrased. One says: they are not called satis who burn themselves with the bodies of the dead. Nanak, they are known as satis who die from the blow of separation. Another: they too are known as satis who live in modesty and contentment, who serve their Lord and rise each morning to remember Him. Look at what he does. He doesn't throw the word away. He keeps it, and he takes it off the pyre. Faithfulness stops being one terrible moment at a funeral and becomes a whole life: modesty, contentment, service, a morning remembered. And the love that's being measured isn't only love for a husband. In the language of the Granth, the soul can be the bride, and the Lord is the Beloved. So the true sati is anyone, woman or man, whose heart aches at being apart from God and who lives faithfully because of it. Tradition remembers Guru Amar Das as speaking against the burning of widows, and it remembers the Sikh Gurus honoring the dignity of women in their sangats. Today's text is part of that memory, in the Guru's own words. It's gentle in its tone and firm in its meaning. Notice also who the salok has in view: a woman in grief. The Guru's answer is to say: live. Your faithfulness counts in a living life, not in ashes. That's the line for today.
screen: `NOT THOSE WHO BURN.` · `MODESTY, CONTENTMENT, SERVICE.` · `THE SOUL AS THE BRIDE.` · `LIVE: FAITHFULNESS IN A LIFE.` · then, large: `NOT THE PYRE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a widow. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who has lost a husband, a wife or a partner. A grandmother, a neighbor, a friend's mom, someone at work. Hold them for a while, without pity. Notice what their life still holds: the way they keep going, the people they look after, the small faithful things they do. Then let one simple gesture come to mind: a call, a visit, a word of thanks, a question about the person they lost. If you pray, you can hold them in Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Who is a true sati. Not the one who burns on the pyre, says Guru Amar Das, but the one who lives in modesty, contentment and service, and aches to be near the Lord. Today's word.
screen: `WHO IS A TRUE SATI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not the pyre. Today, make the gesture you found in the sit, for someone who is carrying on after a loss. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs cite these saloks of Guru Amar Das from the Var of Raga Suhi in katha and in teaching about the Gurus' stand on the dignity of women and widows, and on the Gurus' rejection of widow burning.

fork.setup: a word honors faithful women, and is also used to push grieving widows onto the pyre. you're the Guru. what do you do with the word?
options: keep the word, and give it to the faithful who live.
fork.reveal: Guru Amar Das keeps sati and changes who it belongs to: not those who burn, but those who live in faithfulness.

original.note: a faithful woman; Guru Amar Das gives the name to those who live faithfully, not those who burn.

trapdoor: what you thought: sati is only the name of a cruel old practice.
what it means: the Guru gives the word to the faithful who live, not the widows who burn.
what a scholar hears: in the Granth the soul can be the bride, so the true sati can be anyone who longs for God.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Suhi ki Var, saloks Mahala 3, Ang 787 (satian eh na akhian; those who live in modesty and contentment)

notes: Editor pass: cut unsourced history claims (sati 'praised by some as the height of devotion'; widows' standing in families) and the frequency claim 'the soul is often the bride'.
Both saloks are paraphrased from memory; please check wording and that both sit on Ang 787 in the Suhi ki Var.

The hook's description of the word sati (both 'a faithful woman' and the name for widow burning) and of the practice in 'parts of the society he lived in' is a general history note; please confirm it is fair and does not single out any community.
Tradition that Guru Amar Das spoke against widow burning is attributed to tradition; please confirm.
The teach reads the bride image as the soul longing for God, so the true sati can be anyone; a Keeper may want to adjust this gloss.
